title: India Goes Directly to Iran to Secure Passage for Nine Trapped Tankers and 198 Stranded Sailors
excerpt: With three Indian seafarers dead and an Indian supertanker forced to U-turn at Hormuz, the Modi government is opening its own diplomatic channel to Tehran — sidestepping a stalled American peace deal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India is negotiating directly with Iran to secure passage for trapped tankers and sailors.
  • Three Indian seafarers have died due to US-Iran tensions in the Gulf.
  • India's crude imports from Russia surged to 2.7 million barrels per day in June.
  • The Strait of Hormuz is crucial, with 90% of India's LPG shipments transiting through it.
  • Higher oil prices are straining India's economy, impacting the rupee and inflation.
India is going directly to Tehran. With nine laden tankers carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas sitting trapped in the Persian Gulf, and 198 Indian mariners onboard waiting for a safe path out, the Modi government is considering bilateral talks with Iran to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz — a move that signals how far the escalating US-Iran standoff has pushed New Delhi toward its own diplomatic channel. People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that India's foreign ministry will contact Iranian authorities specifically about the safety of Indian seafarers in the region, hundreds of whom have been stranded for months since the strait was effectively sealed during the US-Iran war that began in February. The calculation is personal as well as strategic. At least three Indian seafarers were killed in American strikes on commercial ships in the Gulf of Oman in June, incidents that prompted India to lodge a formal protest with Washington and summon the US Chargé d'Affaires, Jason Meeks, to the foreign ministry. "We conveyed that the welfare of our seafaring community is very important, and the attacks that are happening must stop," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at the time. ## A One-Clause War The crisis revolves around a single paragraph. Paragraph 5 of the Versailles memorandum of understanding, signed with considerable fanfare on June 17, states that "the Islamic Republic of Iran will make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait. The text makes Iran responsible for opening the waterway — and Tehran has seized on that language to claim sovereign control. "The Strait of Hormuz will only open with 'Iranian arrangements,' not American threats," Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on social media this week. Washington reads the same clause differently. A US official told the Wall Street Journal that the two sides are on "different planets" in their interpretation. Notably, the paragraph says nothing about the US making arrangements for safe passage — an ambiguity Iran has exploited to fire on vessels using American-coordinated routes along the Omani coast. The result, as of Friday, is that daily tanker traffic through Hormuz has slowed sharply. The International Energy Agency reported that global oil supply rose by 4.1 million barrels per day in June as shipping tentatively resumed — but remained a staggering 9.4 million bpd below pre-war levels. ## The Indian Tanker That Turned Back The risks are not abstract. On Wednesday, the Indian-flagged Very Large Crude Carrier *Lila Vadinar*, carrying two million barrels of Kuwaiti crude loaded late last week, made a U-turn off the tip of Oman at the Strait of Hormuz. It joined three empty QatarEnergy LNG tankers — *Al Ghariya*, *Duhail*, and *Al Ruwais* — that had also reversed course after maritime authorities raised the transit threat level to "severe." Still, India's largest refiner is not backing down entirely. Indian Oil Corporation has chartered another VLCC, the *Lila Jamnagar*, to load two million barrels of Iraqi crude from Basrah Oil Terminal around July 23, with delivery bound for the eastern ports of Paradip and Chennai. It would be among the first state-refiner Iraqi crude pickups since the strait effectively closed in February. ## Diversification Is Buying Time — But Not for Everything India's crude supply chain has proven surprisingly resilient through the crisis, largely because of a dramatic pivot toward Russian oil. Russian crude imports climbed to about 2.7 million barrels per day in June — more than half of India's total crude imports — cementing Moscow's position as the country's dominant supplier.

"For now, India's crude supply story remains one of diversification and resilience, not immediate scarcity," said Vandana Ritolia, an energy analyst tracking Indian procurement flows. But crude is only part of the picture. Before the war, almost 40 per cent of India's crude imports, 60 per cent of its LNG shipments, and a staggering 90 per cent of its liquefied petroleum gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. While crude has Russian alternatives, LPG and LNG do not have easy short-term substitutes. India had just lifted temporary restrictions on imported natural gas use, buoyed by the tentative resumption of LNG deliveries through Hormuz. Those restrictions may need to come back if the violence persists. "A prolonged period of instability could tighten availability, increase freight costs, and add pressure to regional prices again, as we have seen over the last few months," Ritolia warned. ## Walking the Tightrope For Indian families watching from Houston and Hyderabad alike, the Hormuz crisis cuts two ways. Higher oil prices threaten the rupee, widen India's import bill, and stoke the kind of inflation that has already strained household budgets across both countries. On Wednesday, the Sensex fell 2.1 per cent and the rupee hit a one-month low as the Iran flare-up roiled markets. But the deeper tension is diplomatic. The United States is India's most important strategic partner on defence, technology, and the Indo-Pacific framework. Iran, however, sits on a waterway that feeds India's kitchen stoves and factory floors.
Impact of Hormuz Crisis on India
›Three Indian seafarers killed in Gulf tensions.
›Sensex fell 2.1% amid rising oil prices.
›Rupee hit a one-month low due to market instability.
The decision to explore direct talks with Tehran — even as the Modi government publicly calls for de-escalation and adherence to international law — reflects a pragmatic acknowledgment: the US-Iran peace process has stalled, Indian sailors are dying, and nine tankers are not going to wait for Paragraph 5 to be renegotiated. *Sources: Bloomberg, Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Hindu Business Line, The Indian Eye*
